utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Prosecution, Dermot Groome, Sabine Baur, and Frederic Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, Vladimir Domazet, lead counsel for the accused Mitar Vasiljevic, and Mr. Radomir Tanaskovic, co-counsel in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, can you hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? There's no need to stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sit down, please, sir. I won't ask you that again whilst we're in this court, but if you do have any problems at any time hearing the proceedings, make sure you make that known so we can have it fixed for you. It is absolutely vital that you hear everything that goes on. Now, Mr. Groome, before we take your opening statement, there are a couple of points that I think I should raise with you. So far as I can see, the accused has never pleaded to the amended indictment. If you know to the contrary, you've got to let me know now, but it certainly doesn't appear in any transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that amended indictment was filed at the last court appearance, and he did not plead at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well then, we better make sure that he pleads before you start. The second matter, in relation to sitting hours. As I understand it at this stage, and it may alter, we will not be sharing this court with any other trial. So we will be sitting the usual sitting hours, 9.30 to 11.00, 11.30 to 1.00, 2.30 until 4.00. This week we'll be sitting Monday to Thursday only because of a build-up of pre-trial matters in some other cases that I have to deal with on Friday. Depending upon the speed with which this trial moves, I hope that we may be able to get through it sitting four days or perhaps four and a half days a week. We'll see how we go. I was rather alarmed to read in the latest pre-trial brief that the estimate for the Prosecution case has grown from 15 days to 26 and a half days, but perhaps the discussions we had at the Pre-Trial Conference will have cured some of that problem. It simply cannot be 26 days. That's two months' worth of work, and we don't have that sort of time, and, in any event, we don't want a great deal of repetition. No doubt by the time we have finished the evidence of the witnesses this week, we will have a very good idea of where the issues really do lie in relation to what might be called the chapeau issues. Another matter is this: I was informed on Friday that the accused's family is using the cubicle at the end of the courtroom there to watch the proceedings this week. I hope that we'll be able to accommodate them there for the whole week, but I do point out a problem, that it is possible from that cubicle to see the witnesses, or at least side on, and all but one of the witnesses this week has an order for protective measures in his favour. There have been some screens erected in the cubicle, and there will have to be some checking to see how suitable they are. But I do draw to your attention, Mr. Groome, that there are members of the public - in effect members of the public - in there this week. So you might also keep an eye on what can be done to ensure that the witness is not visible by the naked eye from that room. Finally, Mr. Domazet has filed now his argument in support of the admissibility of the evidence which tends to establish that there were attacks by the Muslims upon the Serbian civilian population, and we require the Prosecution's response to that as soon as possible because, unfortunately, the submissions came later than we thought they would, and this is an issue which probably will arise with the first witness. Have you given any consideration to that yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been occupied with witness preparation last evening. I've read the motion, and I will have papers to the Court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Tomorrow may be too late, if I may say so, because we are going to have it arising with the first witness in cross-examination, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we hear the witness's testimony. I'm not sure it will. But if it does, I'd be prepared to argue it orally at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Domazet has sent a note to say that the accused's family is not here. Is that so, that the accused's family will not be here at any time, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think this week. Next week it is sure that they ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That they will or will not be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, they will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there's obviously somebody in there who is -- I actually see some of our legal officers in there at the moment. They've probably taken possession. Now, Mr. Domazet, this question of pleading to the amended indictment. It is a formal matter, of course. I assume that your client will be pleading not guilty to each of the charges directed to him. Unless you have some objection to it, I propose simply to ask him does he plead guilty or not guilty to all the charges pleaded against him, and we can take a global answer. Have you any problem with doing it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You agree with that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Vasiljevic, you should stand up, please. There has been an amended indictment filed. It, in fact, reduces the extent of the charges against you, but nevertheless, there are a number of charges there against you. You pleaded not guilty to the original indictment. I therefore ask you: Do you plead guilty or not guilty to each of the charges in the amended indictment pleaded against you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sit down, please. Mr. Groome, are you satisfied with that as a satisfaction of technicalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Then now we'll hear what you want to say by way of opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is just one matter that I want to raise. This is Mr. Tanaskovic's first appearance before the Court. I would just -- given the serious situation that faces some of the witnesses, I would just ask has he read the Court's orders regarding protective measures and is he familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a matter I think you can deal with outside the courtroom. I must assume that they will comply with the rules and that Mr. Domazet, who has quite some experience in this Tribunal, will ensure that he has read the orders. But I don't think it's necessary for me to ask him formally in court. Are you giving evidence, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was told this is where I could give my opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I've never seen it done that way before. That's the witness box. But if you want to do it from there, you're welcome to do so, provided we can hear you. You better turn the microphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May it please the Court, all they wanted to do was to leave. All they wanted to do was to leave Visegrad. By the 14th of June, 1992, the ethnic cleansing operation in Visegrad was well underway. It was as widespread as it was brutal. Most of the town's Muslims who had already fled once in fear, only to return, had now fled for a second and final time. Those who remained were among the last to believe what they hoped to be impossible had now come to pass. On the 13th of June, a Serb from Koritnik walked over to his Muslim neighbours and announced with surprising straightforwardness, "You have to leave. You are being ethnically cleansed. You must leave for Kladanj." These last remaining Muslims of Koritnik, finally resigned to the awful reality around them, they agreed to leave. When they crossed the old Turkish bridge in Visegrad on the 14th, they were simply looking for the Red Cross. They had been told a bus would be waiting for them to take them to safety. There was no bus. They were told perhaps tomorrow. Their great tragedy began when they met the accused, Mr. Vasiljevic. Mr. Vasiljevic is not the most infamous among the Tribunal's indictees. He is no powerful politician accused of the grand plans of the carnage in Bosnia. He is a simple waiter, one generally liked by Muslims and Serbs alike. But he is one who, by his own hands, committed an act which is perhaps one of the single most horrific and egregious affronts to humanity in the war, to the most innocent of victims. Judge Hunt, Judge Janu, Judge Taya, on behalf of the Prosecutor, Ms. Carla Del Ponte, it is both my legal responsibility and my privilege to stand before you and to describe the evidence the Prosecution intends to present in this case against Mr. Vasiljevic. The crime I am speaking about began when Mr. Vasiljevic offered his help to these desperate, desperate people. He led them to a specific house. He told them to remain there the night. They would be safe. He issued them written authorisation to stay overnight. He told them he worked for the Red Cross, that they would be placed on a bus to safety the first thing in the morning. He would then participate with Milan Lukic and several others in burning those people alive. At least 65 people, mostly women and small, helpless children, were forced into a house on the edge of a creek that had already been prepared with highly flammable liquid and set on fire. There was a small baby among them; she had yet to see her third day of life. Anguished cries from the dying echoed along that gully for two hours after the match was first struck. This was not the first time Mr. Vasiljevic and Milan Lukic had killed Muslims. They, along with others, had marched seven unarmed men to the eastern bank of the Drina River and cowardly shot them in the back until they had believed they had killed all of them. One of those men was an old colleague of Mr. Vasiljevic's. His frantic pleas for mercy to his old friend were silenced by a bullet to the back of his head. The seven men dropped into the river that day. Fate spared two, who will recall that day for you during the course of this trial. Your Honours, before I discuss the crimes themselves, I want to begin my remarks by describing, in a very cursory fashion, the historical context in which the accused committed these crimes. The former Yugoslavia, up until 1991, was a federal state comprised of six different republics. One of those republics, Serbia, included autonomous provinces of Voyvodina and Kosovo. After General Tito's death, the forces that originally held these republics together began to disintegrate, and with that came signs that Yugoslavia, as it had existed for the last several decades, was in danger of coming asunder. The increasingly Serb-oriented federal institutions, including the Yugoslav People's Army engaged in a series of conflicts, first in Slovenia, then in Croatia, and soon therefore in Bosnia - all of this an attempt to create a new country, still called Yugoslavia, in the very midst of the separating republics, bloodily carved in part from the land of two of those republics a new Yugoslavia that would be run by and be home to Serbs and their close allies the Montenegrins. This plan, conceived by Serb political leaders both in Serbia and in Bosnia, was executed in a most brutal fashion by the Yugoslav People's Army working in cooperation with special forces from the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs and paramilitary groups funded by nationalist political parties. They worked in close consultation with local political leaders and local police. The military operations of these Serb forces were coordinated and systematic, and by the end of 1992, this campaign resulted in the deaths or forced displacement of approximately 2 million non-Serbs, who were not welcome in this vision of an ethnically homogeneous Serbian state. The United Nations in a series of resolutions attempted to quench the burgeoning flames of inter-ethnic conflict. It passed and implemented an arms embargo and the former Yugoslavia, which froze the military advantage of the Serbs and left the Bosnians unable to adequately arm themselves. However, as a result of international pressure, the Yugoslav People's Army was forced to withdraw from Bosnia by the 19th of May, 1992. The withdrawal was in large measure illusory, as in fact substantial numbers of army personnel and equipment remained in Bosnia to seamlessly reinvent itself as a Bosnian Serb army called the Army of Republika Srpska. Visegrad. Prior to the Bosnian conflict, Visegrad was a small town in southeastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is one of several towns along the Drina River and today forms part of Republika Srpska. Visegrad has a number of features which ensured that it was of strategic importance during the conflict. First, the municipality is the site of an important hydroelectric dam. This dam not only provided essential electricity but also controlled river levels and prevented flooding in areas downstream. Second, the town was an important transportation hub. It is situated on the main road between Belgrade and Sarajevo; the primary road connecting Titovo Uzice in Serbia and Gorazde and Sarajevo. This road was a vital link for the Uzice Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army with its base camp in Uzamnica. Your Honours, I'd like to draw your attention for the next couple of minutes or minute or so to a photograph, an aerial photograph, and I'd like to point out some of the key locations that will come up in testimony here. Let me start with perhaps the most famous of the features of Visegrad; and this is the old Turkish bridge which traverses the Drina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will have to get a microphone around there so they can capture your remarks for the transcript. You are probably speaking at a rate which is the upper limit of their capacity. They are pretty good, but you are speeding a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Drina here runs north, so downstream is going up this way, and this is the direction of north. On the stone bridge, if you recall, or if you take a look, in about the centre, it widens. This is the infamous sofa or the large stone seat where people would pass; as they passed each other, would sit and talk with each other. There is another bridge that crosses the Drina. This is the new bridge. And there was one final bridge that crosses the Rez River [phoen], and this is this bridge here, and you will hear about that. This down here is the football stadium, and you will hear testimony about 4.000 Muslims being gathered here one day to be individually searched and intimidated. Up in this area here is where the two houses, the Pionirska street -- or the three houses that you will hear testimony about on Pionirska street. Perhaps the easiest way to find them is to look across the street from this large, white building, which is a school. Down this area here is called the Bikavac settlement, and you'll hear testimony about the men from the river Drina were hiding here for several weeks and this is where they were apprehended the day they were brought to the Drina River. As we come back full circle, we come to the centre of town down here. And in here we have the hotel Visegrad, the police station, and the Panos restaurant is the restaurant where the accused worked and where most of the people knew him from. There are a few items not depicted on this picture. Let me just indicate where they would be, and you will hear them in the testimony here. There is the Uzamnica Barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army. That is on this bank, the eastern bank, or locals would call it the right bank, of the Drina. But it is further south, so it would be off to the left of the photograph. Also not depicted on the photograph would be the water dam, which would be several kilometres upstream and would be off to the left on the map. And then the two other locations which are not depicted on the map which you will hear testimony of, one is the place in Sase where the seven men were taken to be killed. That is located on the right or eastern bank of the Drina River and is located north of the town several kilometres. The one final location I'd like to indicate for you is the Hotel Vilina Vlas, and that is northeast of the town and would be approximately over here. That is where the men were taken to the river. Local Serb units began a mortar bombardment of the town and its surrounding villages on the 6th of April, 1992. Muslim neighbourhoods and villages were predominantly targeted. In retaliation, a small group of Bosnian Muslim men seized control of that dam that I've just referred to, and they threatened to blow it up. As the Yugoslav army's circle around the town grew closer, one of these men managed to release water from the dam, causing flooding to some houses and streets. This crisis attracted considerable media attention, and leaders on both sides entered into intense negotiations. Many residents, both Serb and Muslim, fled from the town to await the outcome of the crisis. The crisis at the dam was defused when JNA commandos seized the dam. They were followed the next day by a large contingent from the Uzice Corps from the Yugoslav army which had crossed the border from Serbia. The Uzice Corps encountered some light resistance from Muslim factions but ultimately had little difficulty in taking control of the town. After taking control, the JNA positioned tanks and heavy artillery around the town. The JNA detained men and women for questioning. Some of these detainees reported being beaten. After securing absolute control of the town, JNA officers and Muslim leaders, persuaded by assurances from the Yugoslav People's Army that Muslims would be safe, jointly led a media campaign to encourage Muslims to come out from hiding, to return to their homes, to return to their jobs. Many did return, believing in the assurances that they were given and naively hoping that life in Visegrad could once again return to normal. But soon after their return, they learned that this Visegrad was worse, even more threatening than before. Checkpoints manned by army, police, and paramilitaries seemed to be everywhere. People were robbed by police and paramilitaries and threatened with their lives if they did not surrender their property. Local Serbs were sent off for training and practice in shooting weapons. Muslims with prominent positions in the town were fired; some disappeared. Paramilitaries drove around the town playing tapes of people being tortured, from loudspeakers mounted on the tops of their cars. This situation only became worse when the Uzice Corps left the town around the 19th of May, 1992. Upon their departure, local Serb leaders established the Serbian Municipality of Visegrad and took control of the municipal government offices. Soon thereafter, local Serbs, police, and paramilitary units began one of the most brutal campaigns of ethnic cleansing in the Bosnian conflict. This was designed to permanently rid the town of its over 13.000 Bosnian Muslim residents. During the period that followed, Serb and Bosnian Serb forces attacked and destroyed a number of Bosnian Muslim villages. Hundreds of unarmed Muslim civilians in the town of Visegrad were killed for no other reason other than their ethnicity. The Drina was regularly used to dump the bodies of men, women, and children who were killed along its banks or on the historic Turkish bridge, a symbol for centuries of festering animosity between Muslim and Serb peoples. Many of these shockingly mutilated bodies washed down the Drina, where they were caught by a sharp bend in the river near the village of Slap. Many Muslims who were not killed were detained at various locations in town, including the JNA military barracks at Uzamnica. Some were detained in the Hotel Vilina Vlas or other makeshift detention centres. Here the victims were beaten, tortured and subjected to sexual assaults. Many were eventually killed. Both of the town's two mosques were completely destroyed. During the spring of 1992, a former inhabitant of Visegrad, Milan Lukic, returned to Visegrad and took control of a paramilitary unit which worked with the police and military units in exacting a reign of terror upon the local Muslim civilian population. This paramilitary organisation was often referred to by locals as the White Eagles and included Milan Lukic's cousin Sredoje Lukic and his kum, Serbian word for "best man," the accused, Mitar Vasiljevic. Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic were good friends, and their families shared a special bond and relationship that extended over several generations. Sredoje Lukic was a member of the Visegrad police, and Mitar Vasiljevic was a well-known waiter that worked for the Panos company which had several restaurants and coffee houses in the Visegrad area. From April 1992 until October of 1994, Milan Lukic and his group committed hundreds of crimes in the municipality of Visegrad against its non-Serb population. Many of his victims were thrown -- killed on and thrown off the old Turkish bridge, most by the stone sofa. From here the bodies drifted down to Slap, where they were dragged in from the river and given a semblance of a proper Muslim burial. Sadly, the story of Visegrad is one of the most successful stories of ethnic cleansing during the Balkan crisis. Of its over 21.000 people, over 61 per cent were Muslim. During the war, after the events that you will hear about at this trial, there were none left. That is, over 12.000 people forcibly removed from their homes or killed according to the records of the Red Cross. Visegrad holds the tragic distinction of having the most number of people who simply disappeared after Srebrenica, most of them men and teen-aged boys, most of them in May and June of 1992, when the accused made his contribution to this evil scheme. Part of my legal burden is to prove that what Mitar Vasiljevic is accused of wasn't simply the work of a rogue band of criminals but was connected to the takeover and ethnic cleansing orchestrated by Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, and others. The Prosecution will introduce several pieces of evidence on this issue. There are two in particular I would like to tell you about at this time. You will hear from a man who was a prominent member of the Visegrad community. He will describe a chilling event in which he was brought into the command post of the Yugoslav People's Army for a meeting with an army colonel, and as he sat waiting at a table, three officers unknown to him came in and sat at the table across from him. Not realising he was a Muslim, they ignored him. One of them unrolled a map of the town and pointed out to the other two the areas along the right bank that had been successfully cleaned. A paralysis overcame this man as the officer pointed to the village in which his entire family lived on the left bank of the river and declared that it was scheduled for cleaning the very next day. You're also going to see a video taken about five or six weeks before these crimes were committed. It was first aired on Serbian television and begins with a camera crew filming Visegrad from an army helicopter. You will see the helicopter circle over an army facility on which Muslims are gathered onto a concrete basketball court like sheep. The video will continue, and you will see an army truck with armed soldiers in the back and a number of Muslims in the truck. As the truck passes the camera, you can see their frightened, worried faces. One of those frightened people will appear before you. He will describe the day the army entered his village and collected all of the Muslims and brought them to the football stadium in town. He will describe how, as he crossed the old Turkish bridge in the back of that truck that he was driving in, he became part of a line of army trucks also laden with frightened Muslim men, women, and children. He will tell you how the paramilitaries, including these White Eagles, waited at the end of the bridge, jeering and threatening them, unchecked by the great number of army personnel. He will tell you the army made no effort to stop one of the White Eagles as he took his friend's son from the truck in front of him, never to be seen again. I would like to describe in greater detail the crimes for which the accused is about to stand trial. Credible and reliable eyewitness testimony will be adduced that on the 7th of June, 1992, Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and other members of Milan Lukic's group detained seven Muslim civilian men, drove them to the bank of the Drina River, and shot at them. Five of those victims died as a result of the shooting; two escaped fatal injury by pretending to be dead. The events leading to the shooting began at approximately 5.30 in the evening of the 7th, when Milan Lukic and his men were conducting house-to-house searches for Bosnian Muslim civilian men. One of the first men to be taken prisoner was forcibly taken from his own house, and as he was being lead away, he meekly requested permission to give his daughter a good-bye kiss. Milan Lukic said no. When Lukic turned his back, he stole a last kiss from this little girl. The first two men they took prisoner were placed in the rear seat of a dark red Volkswagen Passat that Milan Lukic was known to drive and had been stolen from a Muslim businesswoman who was one of the first to be killed. At approximately the same time, six different men in Lukic's group were at other Muslim homes close to the Bikavac Hotel. Two of the men who were captured had lived for several weeks in the basement of a home, hiding behind a cupboard every time they heard a car drive down the street. When one of these men saw his own car curiously rolling down the street with its engine off, he stepped outside for a closer look, never realising that several of Milan Lukic's men were making their way up the hill behind where he was hiding. Apprehended, they were held with Milan until Milan Lukic arrived. They were brought to another house close by where they were joined by several other unfortunate men who were unable to escape. When Milan Lukic arrived at this area, the Bosnian prisoners were searched and their valuables and identification papers were taken. Perhaps of the first indication of Lukic's intentions was what he did with the identification papers afterwards. He threw them on the ground and kicked them into a pile behind the door. The men were then forced into two cars stolen from Bosnian Muslims. The two cars drove off down through the town, past the two destroyed mosques in the direction of the Vilina Vlas Hotel, north-east of the town. On the way, Milan Lukic stopped as people -- stopped next to people walking in the treatment, and he called out to them from the car, asked them what their name was to see if they were Muslims. At one of the checkpoints that they passed through, he remarked to the police officer there, "I have hunted myself several balijas," a derogatory word used to describe Muslims. When the two cars filled with the Bosnian Muslim prisoners arrived at the closed and empty Vilina Vlas Hotel, they were met by the accused, Vasiljevic, and other members of Milan Lukic's group. The accused was standing at the left of the lobby as they entered. The accused was well known to the victims from his many years of work as a waiter in several restaurants and coffee houses owned by the Panos company in Visegrad. One of the victims, Meho Savovic, had been Vasiljevic's supervisor and his mentor in the company. The accused was dressed in an olive drab military uniform with a red ribbon on the sleeve. Both his black cap and uniform bore the insignia of a double-headed eagle. He was armed with an automatic rifle. While the men were lined up with their backs to the reception desk, Mitar Vasiljevic stood on their right while another Serb guard stood on their left. Milan Lukic rummaged through the reception desk in an futile attempt to look for a certain set of keys. He opened the door behind the reception desk and looked there as well. When he couldn't find the keys he was looking for, he angrily exclaimed, "Let's go back." The seven men were once again forced into the two cars. The accused, Vasiljevic, sat in the front passenger seat of the Passat as Milan Lukic drove. The two vehicles drove to Sase, a small village just outside Visegrad and just along the bank of the Drina River. On the way, one of the paramilitaries offered one of the men a cigarette and assured him, "You are being taken to be exchanged." As they pulled alongside the road in front of a house, Milan Lukic asked Vasiljevic if he knew whether the house was owned by Muslims. He replied that it was. After the accused and the other paramilitaries got out of the car, they assumed positions around the car and ordered the Bosnian Muslims out. Milan Lukic had a sniper's rifle with a sound suppressor or silencer, and Mitar Vasiljevic had a locally made Kalashnikov-style rifle like the other two men. All of the guns, including the one held by Mr. Vasiljevic, were trained on the men. When the captives were out of the car, they were forced to walk towards the Drina, which was approximately 100 metres away. On the way to the river, Milan Lukic and Mr. Vasiljevic guarded their condemned on one side and the remaining paramilitaries guarded them from the other. It was clear to the men what fate awaited them. One of them attempted to move towards his brother-in-law as they walked to say a last good-bye. He was quickly threatened to walk straight ahead. When they arrived at the river, the seven men were ordered to line up along its bank. The men walked the ten paces slowly towards the river they swam in as boys, knowing that to reach it was to meet their death. Vasiljevic's former supervisor, Meho Savovic, repeatedly begged the accused to spare his life. Vasiljevic coldly responded, "I don't know you." Some of the others begged as well, but it was in vain. Some of them were simply silent and spent what they thought was the last few moments of their life thinking about their children or the others they had loved. As the seven stood at the river's edge, Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, and the other paramilitaries assumed positions approximately ten metres behind them. After a brief discussion regarding whether to use the Kalashnikovs in automatic or semi-automatic mode, the sound of the three guns could be heard as they were clicked into single shot. The paramilitaries, beginning with Milan Lukic, fired repeatedly into the men's backs and into their heads until they believed they had killed all of them. Two of the victims threw themselves into the river when the firing began and desperately pretended to be dead. They remained still in the shallow water as additional shots were fired into the bodies around and on top of them to ensure that they had all been killed. They could hear the sound of the bullets thud into the bodies of their friends. They could feel life quickly leave the men lying on them as their movement stilled. When the paramilitaries were satisfied that they had killed the seven men, Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, and the others returned to the two cars and drove away. The two survivors of the shooting remained motionless until they heard the cars leave, and together they found their way to safety. For these crimes, Mr. Vasiljevic has been charged with murder as a crime against humanity and as a violation of the laws or customs of war, the crime of inhumane acts as a crime against humanity, and finally the crime of violence to life and person as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The evidence of this incident will come from four sources,

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There will also be testimony from a man who was hiding on the opposite bank and observed the crime through a set of binoculars. And finally, by the accused's own account of what happened, I will talk in greater length about his videotaped interview. But for now I will just say that he admits being present at all times during the crime beginning from the Vilina Vlas hotel through the executions themselves and up until Milan Lukic dropped him back at his home. The fire. Credible and reliable eye witness testimony will establish beyond a reasonable doubt that on or before the 14th of June, 1992 approximately 65 to 75 people of Bosnian Muslim ethnicity, mostly women and children, were imprisoned in a house on Pionirska street by Mr. Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and then burned alive. The events leading up to the fire began as a group of people, mostly women and their children from a small settlement called Koritnik, about six kilometres outside of Visegrad, gathered in the town of Visegrad, seeking the protection of the Red Cross and a way to leave the town. Earlier in the day, one of their Serb neighbours told them directly that the village was to be ethnically cleansed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Some of these people had been instructed earlier in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we've had another request to please slow down. When you are reading, it's very natural for to you speed up. I'm told I do it myself. But just keep it in mind. It has to be translated or interpreted and it has to be typed, so just space yourself out a little more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Some of these people had been instructed earlier in the day by people claiming to work for the Red Cross or a refugee committee that there would be safe transportation out of the town. The accused Mitar Vasiljevic was among those who disseminated this false information and falsely represented himself to be a member of the Red Cross. Most of these people had been forced from their homes or had determined that remaining in Visegrad imperiled their lives. Finding the Red Cross office closed, the group made its way to a Muslim neighbourhood at the edge of Visegrad where they hoped to find shelter for the night. As they approached the area, they were met by Vasiljevic, who introduced himself by name and told them that he was working for the refugee commission. Most of them already knew him from his work in the Panos restaurants. Vasiljevic instructed the women to stay in the ransacked house of Jusuf Memic on Pionirska street and issued them an official looking certificate supposedly legitimising this arrangement. He returned one more time later in the day and assured them that they would be safe there and that, in the morning, transportation would be arranged to carry them out from Visegrad. Shortly after Mr. Vasiljevic's second instruction to the group, Milan and Sredoje Lukic, the men that he had worked with in the past, as well as another from that group, arrived. They stole valuables from the group, questioned them about their husbands, and then made them strip naked for a final, humiliating search. When they finished, they again instructed them, as Vasiljevic had done before, they were to remain in the house until morning. Later that day, Milan and Sredoje Lukic returned to the house and forced the shoeless victims to move to another house behind the first house, a house owned by Adem Omeragic. This house was only 20 to 50 metres away and was closer to the stream that ran behind the houses. There were already a number of persons detained in this house, and the group from the Memic house had to be physically squeezed into the Omeragic house. It was clear to one of the witnesses when she entered that the carpet had been soaked with some volatile chemical and the windows had been barricaded. The chemicals smelled like glue and it made it difficult to breathe. After approximately 30 minutes, Milan and Sredoje Lukic and Vasiljevic came back to the house and opened the front door. As Vasiljevic and Sredoje Lukic stood at Milan Lukic's sides preventing anyone from escaping, Milan Lukic placed an explosive device on the carpet and lit its fuse. As the device exploded, it ignited the flammable substance on the floor. The flames quickly engulfed the solvent-soaked socks of the victims and the house itself. Vasiljevic and the Lukics remained outside the house, shooting at any of the people who desperately tried to escape through the windows. One woman and her son climbed out of the window and fled along the creek bed. Another young boy showed him mother to that very same window and jumped out first and ran as quickly as he could down the creek bed and up to a small hill across the creek. He did not see his mother climb out after him. He did not see when she was shot by Milan Lukic. She rolled down the embankment of the stream, limp from her wounds. As she lay there, she listened to the horrifying screams of the victims as they burnt to death. Her son on the crest of that hill could not see her and cried as he watched the house burn, listening to the screams of his many burning relatives, believing that his mother was among them. It would not be until 1995 that he would learn that his mother had survived that Holocaust. The two Memic houses were also burned to the ground that night. For these crimes, Mr. Vasiljevic has been charged with extermination, murder, both as a crime against humanity and as a violation of the laws and customs of war, the crime of inhumane acts as a crime against humanity, and finally the crime of violence to life and person as a violation of the laws and customs of war. There is also an overall charge of persecution regarding the totality of the accused's conduct. The Pionirska evidence. The evidence of what happened on Pionirska street will come from a number of sources. Remarkably, seven people escaped the fire that day. As the women were moved from the Memic house to the Omeragic house, two sisters, two twins, dropped behind a shed as they passed by -- as they passed by the shed as the group was forced into the second house. They will describe their observations of the fire, the crime in general, and in particular their observation of the accused, Mr. Vasiljevic, and his participation in the crime. Of the approximately 70 people that were forced into the house -- I'm sorry, of the people that escaped, two mothers and their sons were able to climb out of the window and jump to the ground. They will come and testify about their ordeal and the role the accused played in the crime. An elderly man also survived the fire that night, a man who knew and identified Mr. Vasiljevic very soon after the fire. Although he died in 1995, we will call his son to recount what his father told him about the fire that night. Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to another enlarged photograph - this is an aerial photograph of the Pionirska street houses that are relevant to this trial - and just point out a couple of things. These two houses here are the houses that belong to the Memics. They are most easily identified by the northerly one which has a green and yellow awning at this point in time, and as you can see, they are directly across from the large, white school which can be seen on the broader shot. These houses were burned that night, but these are not the houses where the women were forced into and burned. That is this house back here, this shell of a house back here. And in particular, the witnesses will talk about this bottom, ground floor with no windows on this side, simply windows facing the creek which runs along, through, or under the shade of these trees. The ashes of these and remains of the dead are still in and around that house. And in a final act of desecration, the ground floor of the house was turned into a pig sty that -- today that hallowed ground lies covered in pig filth. From very early on in the Prosecution case, I think you will have a sense of just how well known Mr. Vasiljevic was. You will hear ample evidence regarding how the witnesses know Mr. Vasiljevic. One woman will tell you she has known him all her life. They are about the same age. They were born in the same area. As young adults, they used to frequent the same places, and she, like the rest, knew him from the Panos restaurants and cafes. One of the witnesses will tell you how often he frequented the cafe where Mr. Vasiljevic worked and will estimate that he has seen Mitar Vasiljevic hundreds of times over the course of the last several years, prior to 1992. At least one of the defences in this case, perhaps the primary defence, is that the accused was not present when the fire was actually set in Pionirska street. Because this necessarily raises the issue of whether or not the witnesses were mistaken, the Prosecution undertook to conduct identification procedures in this case. The format of the identification procedure was a photo array. I have placed one of these arrays on the ELMO, and I would ask if we can see that now. Each witness, along with the investigator and interpreter, was asked to view a set of pictures. The photo array contained a picture of the accused along with a number of other men of similar appearance, one of which was a recent photograph of the accused. They were asked if they recognised anyone. If they did, they were asked who they recognised it to be. They were then asked to sign their name to the photograph they recognised. The investigators will testify and describe the steps they took to ensure that the identification procedure was fair. And you will hear from the witnesses themselves, describe the circumstances under which they were shown the photo spread and the level of certainty they had in identifying the picture that they did. An alibi defence has been raised in relation to Pionirska street. The accused in his video statement claims that on the day of the 14th, he fell off a horse in the centre of town. He says that he found the horse abandoned northeast of the town and rode it into the town to release it along the railroad tracks and in the very centre of town, the horse slipped, threw him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I couldn't read the signature there, but in case somebody could, is that a witness who has protective measures in his or her favour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour, it is a witness who has protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suggest you don't show it on the ELMO any more unless you want it somehow in private session. But I think we've seen enough of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. At the very centre of the town, the horse slipped, threw him, and then fell on top of him, breaking his leg. And sure enough, there are medical records from Uzice hospital which indicate that a person by the name of Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted into the hospital that night at approximately 11.00 p.m., here in this book. Some jurists might be tempted to end the inquiry here. It is a seemingly impressive piece of evidence, and there is no obvious evidence that it was forged or tampered with. But the victims of this fire are owed more than a cursory look, a summary decision about this piece of evidence important to the case. This big blue ledger was not the only item contained in the medical records. You will hear about all of the documents contained in the records and the circumstances under which they came into the possession of OTP. If this inquiry is to be a complete one, then they all must be examined carefully. In one of the admittance records, a doctor or nurse noted where the person had broken his leg and it said, "the battlefield." In the box for indicating who was notified of the person's injury, there is an indication that a military post was notified. There was also an x-ray film of the person's broken leg. Written across the bottom of the x-ray, very clearly, is the name Mitar Vasiljevic and the date, 14 June 1992. You will hear testimony from Dr. DeGrave, an expert in the comparison of x-rays. He will describe how he had the opportunity to conduct a physical and radiological exam of the accused this past August. He will also describe his analysis and comparison of an x-ray of the accused's leg taken here in the prison with the one that was part of the medical records. He will tell you that, to a scientific certainty, the leg depicted in the x-ray from the Uzice hospital is not the same person as the accused. You will hear from two women that helped one of the survivors of the Pionirska street fire. They tended her burns and injuries soon after the fire. You will hear them describe their encounter with Mr. Vasiljevic after they saw the woman who survived the fire. Your Honours, this process we embark on this morning will hopefully lead us to the truth of what Mr. Vasiljevic's participation was in the Pionirska street fire. The Prosecution's role in that process has been to thoroughly investigate this matter and gather relevant evidence. I think at the conclusion of the Prosecution's case, you will see that this has been done. And in that search for evidence, evidence was discovered that suggest that these records are not what they seem. That will be presented. There is also evidence that suggests that perhaps the accused was indeed in that hospital. That evidence was promptly turned over to Mr. Domazet, Defence counsel for the accused, and I trust that he shall present that evidence in turn. All the Prosecution ask of Your Honours at this juncture is to reach no hasty conclusion, forge no theory about what happened, until you have heard all of the evidence and both counsel have had an opportunity to address you. Further in relation to Defence assertion that Mr. Vasiljevic is not guilty because he was not present when the fire was ignited, I would say the following: Your Honours, Mr. Vasiljevic did not begin his part in this crime when he shone a flashlight on the victims so Milan Lukic could shoot them. His part in this crime did not begin when he guarded the door as Milan Lukic knelt to ignite the carpet under the feet of the victims. His part did not start when he helped move them from the house on the road to the house where they died. This crime began when he told the victims to go stay in that first house. This crime began when he issued a supposed official document authorising them to stay in this house. This crime began when he told them he worked for the Red Cross and they would be safe there that night. It is just common sense that perpetrators of crimes tell lies to their victims. The kidnapper tells the young child that he has candy for her. Why, even the first murder recorded in the Bible, Cain invited his brother Abel to go for a walk, to lure him away to be killed. Like so many crimes before, the victims of this fire were told lies to overcome their resistance to what Mr. Vasiljevic and the two Lukics had planned for them. I draw your attention to them in advance. They will be important in this case. You will hear evidence that not only in the Pionirska street but also in the Drina river, you will hear a witness describe an event that she witnessed in which she saw Mr. Vasiljevic take a young little girl who was crying for her father and put the little girl up on his lap.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, another complaint. I realise you're probably trying to finish this speedily, but we'd rather have it taken properly by the interpreters and the court reporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He cuddled this small girl who was crying for her father. He consoled her with a smile and told her that her dad had been taken to be exchanged. Her father's butchered body was one of the ones that washed up in Slap. Your Honours, I suspect that it is quite possible at some point in this case you may be struck by the idea that this case really isn't about whether these witnesses are mistaken when they saw Mr. Vasiljevic commit those horrific acts on the 14th of June. You just may conclude that they could not be mistaken; they know him too well. You may be drawn to the dilemma that this case isn't about mistake, it's about some person or persons attempting to perpetrate a fraud upon this Tribunal. Someone must not be telling the truth. In that likelihood, I would ask, as we begin to hear testimony today, that you closely assess the credibility of each and every witness for the Prosecution. Consider the risks that they have accepted to come to tell you what Mr. Vasiljevic did. Consider the magnitude of how difficult it is to relive that night here in court. Look carefully into their eyes and see the scars from the fire that night and ask yourself whether or not you believe them. In 1961, a native Visegradian by the name of Ivo Andric won the Nobel Prize for literature for his famous book, "The Bridge over the Drina," a book about this bridge, this town, and these people. He describes the bluish green Drina rushing northward out of the precipitous gorge and the old, stone Turkish bridge which traverses it, connecting its flattened banks where the town of Visegrad was founded so many years ago. He describes life there among the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats and how from time to time an inexplicable madness descends like a poisonous fog on the town, dividing its several peoples and giving birth to egregious acts of violence, many of them, and the cold stone seat of the bridge, that sacrificial altar to an insane god of nationalism. Why, in June of 1992 Mitar Vasiljevic and the Lukics decided to write the next chapter of that book, a chapter far surpassing any one that came before it in its complete and utter cruelty to the most innocent of victims, we can never hope to understand. Fortunately, the law does not impose upon me the burden of proving what compelled Mr. Vasiljevic to commit these acts. The law does impose upon me the burden of proving that he did in fact intentionally commit these crimes, a burden that will be satisfied completely by the evidence that will be presented over the coming weeks. They just wanted to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now that you're back at your usual position, Mr. Groome, may I ask you just two questions? What was the street in which the burnt house is to be found? Was it Pionirska, or if it was, what is the street in which the other buildings are shown, the ones opposite the school? Because we are going to get into terrible trouble if we keep on referring to this as the Pionirska street incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Pionirska street here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. That's where the house was when they were first put.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: First brought. The other house isn't on the street. It's essentially in the backyard of these houses here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, I was tempted at first to call them the first and the second house, but then we are going to get into trouble because of the way in which you have drafted the indictment, because there is another house in Pionirska street that was burnt -- no, in another street that was burnt. It's referred to throughout as the second house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That we call these two houses the Memic houses. They were owned by the Memics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, please let's keep it either a street number or the street name, but the names of people are very difficult to keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, in this part of the world, this house did not have a street number or even a street. You must walk through the backyard to get to it. It's just on a creek bed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can we call that the backyard house? It's just much easier to have names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Call it the house by the creek?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: House by the creek? All right. Don't mind. Whichever way you like. The other question I wanted to ask you: It appears you are grasping the nettle, as it were. You're going to deal with the alibi in the Prosecution's case in chief, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that's all right. Now, Judge Taya would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I want to have some clarification from the Prosecution. As to the house-burning incident on Pionirska street, according to the opening statement of the Prosecutor, there are already a number of persons in the house of Adem Omeragic when approximately 65 Bosnian Muslims arrived there. As to those persons who were already in the house of Adem Omeragic, is it the allegation of the Prosecutor that they were also detained there by the accused, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic and others? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately we know very little about those people. Those people were not from the village of Koritnik. The victims in this case from the village of Koritnik did not recognise them. I think there will be a reasonable inference that they -- it was all part of the same conduct by Mr. Lukic and Mr. Vasiljevic, but there will be no evidence about the identity of those people or how they came to be in that house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you may call your first witness. What are we going to do about all of the documents that we're eventually going to get? I assume we're going to be given some documents, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour called my assistant Friday afternoon, and I believe they were prepared the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I made no calls, but certainly one of the legal officers did because usually we get them in advance. Are we going to be given a copy of each of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How have you got them identified in the folders?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, they're in the order that we intend to refer to them. They've all been pre-numbered. I was going to ask for a few minutes with the clerk of the court to decide whether we pre-mark them all for identification at this juncture or we do it as we call upon the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be sufficient if you just leave the numbers on it. We will use those numbers as exhibit numbers for ease of reference. If any are not tendered or not admitted into evidence, then we just simply will not have any exhibits of that number. I don't think it's necessary to mark them for identification as such. There will be some documents which will be marked for identification which won't get into evidence immediately, perhaps because some other witness has to establish their authenticity. But if you have numbers on the documents, we'll keep to those numbers. At this stage, they are simply numbered documents, but we will use those numbers for the exhibit numbers. They're going to be tendered when you call the investigator, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Some, and some will be referred to when the witnesses testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We haven't seen the investigators' names on the list yet, so I assume that some of these witnesses will be referring to plans or streets, maps, or something like that, will they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, could we have those at some stage before the witnesses come?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They can be provided for you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps during the morning adjournment you can physically supply them to us. Let's see how we go with your first witness though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask for just a couple of minutes to rearrange the witness box and recover some of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly. And you can take that down so the interpreters can see what's going on inside the courtroom. They do really need to see. The technical people will be pleased to set up the witness box again after you've destroyed its virginity. I'm sure it's the first time it's ever been used by counsel for an address. So it won't take long. The technical people can come in and fix up the microphones. Who is your first witness? I gather there is some problem with your witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG022, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, this witness is going to have facial distortion and a pseudonym. Yes, very well. When you are doing your list, it would be very helpful if you did it the same way as the one we received on Friday noting what the protective measures are, because otherwise we have to go searching through the books. Are we getting somebody from the audio-visual group to come and fix the microphones, or are we allowed to do them ourselves? Mr. Groome, I notice there's a reference there that this witness is expected to give us some idea of the political situation after the multi-party elections. How far are we going to go into this? It really only invites what the Defence wants to do, to run the line that it was an attack by the Muslims upon the Serbs. Why do we have to go into so much detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask him to give a very brief description of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But a very brief description is going to invite, then, a brief description about something else. You've got an admission there was an armed conflict at the relevant time. We can assume that. Somebody, I assume, will give us a brief history which will support your opening address how the former Yugoslavia split up. I don't know what more we need, except, of course, you have to prove that it was an international armed conflict if you're still pursuing that particular set of charges. Most of the smaller cases such as this, that has been dropped, and I'm still hoping that you might see some common sense about that. But what we are going to end up doing is a long argument about meetings, political rallies, and what was said in parliament and all of this, and I'm at a loss myself to know why we need that. All we have to prove -- all we have to have proved for us is that there was an attack upon the Muslim civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness will not be going into the items that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be a relief, because I've heard them so often now when Prosecutions have forced it on us. Is the witness ready? Yes, bring him in then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. There were no Article 2 points on this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Aren't there? I thought that there was some discussion in the pre-trial brief about the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, will you stand up to take the solemn declaration that the usher is showing you? Please stand up so that the usher can show you the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Who is taking this witness? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me? Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just say yes so we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take off your jacket. You're going to be here awhile. Get yourself comfortable, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, have you got what has generally been described as a pseudonym sheet that shows his name and address or his name and age and place of birth, which also shows his pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a list of all names and all the pseudonyms that have been assigned in this case. I do not have the biographical information on it. If you like, I will provide that for you this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The way I have found it always to be done - and it is far more helpful if it is done this way - is that for each witness, you provide a sheet of paper which has his name and whatever identification details you want in it, plus a reference to his pseudonym, and then he knows that he will be referred to by that pseudonym. And then you have on that sheet of paper a list of all of those persons to whom he may refer who have pseudonyms. You can't expect every witness to go through a whole list of pseudonyms to work out whether somebody he's going to mention is on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't expect that of witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, how is he going to know, when he refers to somebody by name, that he shouldn't refer to that person by name but by a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's not going to refer to anybody that he shouldn't refer to by name, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. But for the other witnesses, do you think we can do it? It saves him having to write down on a piece of paper what his name is, and we've got a document which goes in under seal as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the numbering of those exhibits is going to have to follow your numbering system. So can you tell me how far your numbering system goes at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're up around 55 at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's start off, let's say, at 70. So the first pseudonym sheet or whatever other document you will want in will start off at 70. Now, you proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you have been assign the pseudonym VG22. Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you that you've been assigned number 22 and asking are you ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just remind you, as I told you yesterday, please do not use your name or any information about yourself which could identify you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep on interrupting, Mr. Groome, but we have to know what his name is somewhere on the record. That's the purpose of the pseudonym sheet that I suggested to you. It's given to the accused's counsel and to us and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I provided such a table with the protective measures motion. I assumed that that's what the Court would be using this morning to coordinate the numbers with the names. I apologise, and we will have the sheet you're requesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, is that your name on that sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. That will be Exhibit 70. Show it to the accused's counsel, please. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to briefly describe your educational and professional background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I completed primary school in Visegrad, secondary school. I graduated from the high school for air force studies in Mostar, and I graduated from the faculty in Sarajevo. After graduating, I worked in Visegrad, in a local firm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And today what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Today I live in Sarajevo and I have a private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask you to describe for the Court what was the general political situation in Visegrad in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: As has become common knowledge, in 1990 -- that is to say, in the former Yugoslavia and also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the first multi-party elections were held. Up until then, it was a one-party system with one party; that is, the Communist Party. After the multi-party elections were held, there were two parties in Visegrad which gained the largest number of votes and seats and deputies or members of parliament for the town of Visegrad. Those parties were the Party of Democratic Action and the Serbian Democratic Party, and they made up the majority. They had the power. The other parties had negligible influence and had a very small number of deputies in the parliament. In keeping with this, the results of the election, the power, and the authority after the elections was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's 11.00. We'll take the break now. I should have said that Exhibit 70 will be under seal. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall where we left off, or would you like to have the last line of your testimony read back to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I do recall the point where we left off, and we may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: As I was saying, power and authority in the municipality of Visegrad was divided up in percentages and commensurate with the multi-party election results. The assembly of Visegrad numbered 50 members of Parliament or deputies, and of that number, the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, won 27 seats; the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, had 13 seats; and three or four other parties had the rest, making up the 50 number. The SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, Serbian Democratic Party, had wielded power and authority in the municipality to all effects, with the majority. The President of the municipal assembly was Mr. Fikret Cocalic, and his assistant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One moment, sir. We do not need this detail, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of these names will become relevant later on in the trial. I assure you that I will try to keep it as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The fact that, in effect, you're letting the witness have his head worries me. He has a story to tell, but very little of it will be relevant to what we have to decide. So just try to take him to where you want him to go so we can get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of time, when I prepared him yesterday, I asked him to tell briefly. So rather than interrupt him with questions on each point, I'd ask you to give us perhaps a little leeway, and if you want me to start going point by point, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you assure us that it is going to be relevant, he can proceed, but I really do not want to know all of this history. It is not relevant to anything we have to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue. Would you please tell us just the main names of the heads of the two parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Very well. The President of the Party of Democratic Action was Mr. Fikret Cocalic, and other influential members of the party were Omer Brankovic, Ohranovic Esad. I myself was a member of that party. The President of the Serbian Democratic Party was Mr. Branimir Savovic and his assistants were Stanko Pecikoza, Risto Perisic. They were the most influential people in the Serbian party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now: Did there come a time when Muslim members of the Territorial Defence were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen. It happened somewhere in February or March 1992. And how it happened was the following: The Yugoslav People's Army issued an order that all firms, companies, and institutions who had arms in their possession intended for Territorial Defence purposes were to lay down those arms and hand them into the army; that is to say, to the Yugoslav People's Army. And that's what happened during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the company that you worked for at the time, were you a prominent member in that company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I was the manager of that company, or director, and that company had a significant stock of weapons and military equipment which was taken over by the Yugoslav people's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come a time to your knowledge that people of Serb ethnicity were provided arms in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I am aware of that fact, yes, because a large number of people saw that taking place. How it happened was that in -- that vehicles brought in weapons to Serb villages and those weapons were distributed amongst the Serb nationals or ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were members of your company who were Serb, were they given any special military training around this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At that time, practically all the employees in the company that I was director of went for military training, and this military training was conducted by the offices of the Yugoslav People's Army together with the heads of the Territorial Defence who were Serbs by ethnicity. This took place on a training ground which was generally used for military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Chamber when was the first incident of violence or shooting incident in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The first shooting took place on the 4th of April 1992, and it happened some 10 or 12 kilometres away from the centre of town at a place called Dobrun. And I know for sure that it was in a quarry, a stone quarry there, and the workers working in the stone quarry were shot at and they left the quarry and came into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the days after that initial shooting, were there mortar attacks on Muslim areas of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The first day was artillery shooting. On the very next day, there was mortar bombardment, and places inhabited by Muslims were shot at as well as the centre of town. And as the days went by, the shooting became more and more intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd now like to draw your attention: Did there come a time when approximately 12 Serbs were taken or captured by some of the Muslim members of the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This occurred on perhaps the 7th, 8th or 9th of April 1992. It wasn't the Muslim police, but they were units of the police force, the police force that had already been in existence, and members of the Territorial Defence who were doing routine patrolling around town, and they happened to come across an armed group of 12 individuals who were -- neither belonged to the police force or the army or the Territorial Defence, and they arrested them, took them into custody, and took them to the police station in town, where they held them in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I knew most of them personally. Some of those people who had been taken into custody were members of the regular police force, 10 to 15 days previously, in town; whereas some of the others were civilians until 10 or 15 days prior to the event. And I knew them personally. I knew where they worked, what they did, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And at the time they were taken into custody, were they dressed in military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them had the police-type uniforms. Others were wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to describe the events of the next five days. I'm going to ask you to go day by day, beginning with day one, the time when water was released from the dam. Would you explain the circumstances surrounding the release of the water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is an admission of fact about this, is there not? The document that was attached to the pre-trial brief is not signed, and I know there has been some problem about translations of it, but is that not an admitted fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be. And I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know you want to go further, but I'm just trying to say you don't have to prove that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it's not directly relevant to the charges, but it does fill out the picture of what was going on in Visegrad at the time, and I think it will be particularly important to understand the context in which these crimes occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, every time you talk about the picture and the context, I become worried. Unless it proves something, we are not terribly interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to prove a connection between the events as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Then it is relevant. You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Will you please describe the beginning -- let's call this day one, the day water was released from the dam, and tell us the circumstances surrounding that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The water from the dam was released by a certain man called Murat Sabanovic, who came there at his own initiative with a group of men. And the very act of releasing the water was geared towards preventing; that is to say, the threat that water would be released from the dam and the hydroelectric power plant was geared towards turning away the arrival of the Yugoslav People's Army units which were burgeoning towards the town of Visegrad. They were coming in large numbers and from different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you become --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: But as they did not succeed in preventing the army from coming in, I think what happened next was on the 12th of April -- that was the date when he actually released the water from the dam, just before the arrival of the troops, the army troops, before they reached the hydroelectric power plant and the surrounding villages around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you explain to us what would have happened had the water in the dam all been released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Had all the water been released from the dam, I do not think that anything major would have occurred, because downstream on the River Drina, there was another dam which had been emptied previously. So it would have captivated that water. But there would have been local damage in the town and the villages bordering on the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the response of the people who lived in Visegrad to this threat of the water being released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, it caused a great deal of fear and panic amongst the population because they tied this in with the arrival of the army and the release of the water. And as there was fear generally, this made the situation worse. So the fact of the water being released was -- tipped the scale in this balance of fear. They were terribly afraid that if the water was released, everything would be inundated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did members of the Muslim community flee from Visegrad in response to this threat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. The town was left empty on threat that the water would be released. And when a little of it was released, everybody left the town. The town was left completely empty by all its inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
