utterances.text: And where did the Muslim members of Visegrad go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The Muslims from Visegrad went, for the most part, in two directions. One direction was upstream towards the town of Gorazde, and the other direction was downstream towards villages that were five or six kilometres away from the centre. Brstanica was one of them, and it was the centre of this rallying of the population. And a small part went off to Priboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did members of the Serb community also flee the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you mentioned that some water was released from the dam. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, some of the water was released. Not all of it, but some of it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the result of that water being released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The results weren't what people had expected them to be. They were very much afraid. But what happened was that one of the villages suffered mostly, the village where Murat Sabanovic in fact lived, the actual person who released the water; whereas the rest of the damage was not as great.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any loss of life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. When this act took place, nobody lost their lives, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But there was damage to property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were asked to negotiate on behalf of the Muslim population or be involved in negotiations on behalf of the Muslim population to try to reduce tensions in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, negotiations were called for. The first negotiations were called for by the SDS with respect to the release of the 12 people who had been taken prisoner. After that, the Yugoslav People's Army asked for negotiations, which took place in the barracks near Visegrad, and I attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to the first negotiation. Did that occur on the day after the water was released from the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after the water was released, the first negotiations were held with the SDS at a place called Kosovo Polje, perhaps some two kilometres out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In which direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Downstream on the right-hand bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be north of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: North, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please describe for the Court what happened at that negotiation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At the negotiations, the president of the SDS was to come. His name was Branimir Savovic. He was expected to arrive. And on the other side, (redacted) We came to that village. Mr. Branimir Savovic did not arrive, but the negotiations were attended by the Vice-president of the SDS party, Stanko Pecikoza. We discussed the release of the people that had been taken into custody, and our side - if I can use that term - called for a ceasefire, for an end to the mortars shelling Muslim villages and parts of the town, and we said that two days later they would be released. Stanko said that he didn't have the authority to go ahead with anything like that. And we sat around talking for a while because we knew each other from before. We knew each other quite well, in fact. So we discussed the situation. This might have gone on for about an hour, and then we all went our ways, having agreed upon nothing, decided nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber, did you have difficulty arriving at this place or returning back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: As we had agreed to meet at that particular location and hold the negotiations there, the SDS guaranteed safe conduct, that we would not be shot at. I told them which car we would be arriving in and other information of that kind. The only difficulties that we had was because of the water that was released from the dam, because there were pebbles and sludge on the road. That was the only difficulty. We found it difficult to reach the location because of all the sludge and slush and stones on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to move now to day three. Did you have a meeting with a member of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: After one or two days, the President, Mr. Cocalic, that Colonel Ojdanci, who was the commander of the Uzice Corps, wished to talk to the leadership of the municipality, and I said that I would go with them in view of the fact that (redacted) (redacted) and that's what happened. That's how we went to the negotiations which had been scheduled to take place in a barracks called Uzamnica on the right bank of the Drina, two to three kilometres upstream and quite near the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be south of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who else attended from the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: On the part of the Yugoslav People's Army, there was the commander, the local commander of the barracks, and his name was Captain Borko. But he didn't actually attend the negotiations. He was just there. He would come and go for brief periods of time. He would come in and leave, but he didn't actually attend the negotiations. There were other members from the JNA and Colonel Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Uzamnica barracks, was Colonel Ojdanic present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No. We arrived a little earlier. Actually, we arrived on time, at the scheduled time; whereas the colonel was a little late. In the room where the negotiations were to be held, we came across several JNA officers who were not from the barracks themselves, and amongst them there was an air force major, so we talked to them for a while while we were waiting for Colonel Ojdanic to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anything occur between yourself and this major?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: While we were waiting for the colonel - and we waited for approximately one hour - the major was very nervous and angry. He was a little intoxicated. And immediately after the talks started, which refer to the situation in Visegrad, he was angry, he beat the table with his fists, he hurled derogatory terms at our team. I wasn't there alone. I was with some others. So that it was all very unpleasant, and we were a little taken aback by his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time this meeting was being held, who is in control of the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: We went to the negotiations in the barracks via the dam, across the dam, because there was no other way to reach the barracks. There was nobody there, just some of the workers who worked on the dam's maintenance. When the meeting with the colonel was over, on our return, we were detained by soldiers of the JNA, so that means that in the meantime, they had taken control of the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when you were detained by these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, standard procedure. They had their weapons cocked at us. We were told to get out of the car. We were all travelling in small passenger vehicles. They searched the cars. They searched us personally. And they asked us to go by military truck to see the commander who was providing security for the dam. He was Captain Vukosavljevic. He was the dam commander. We insisted on going in our own car and the captain came to see us. That's what happened in the end. After we had explained who we were and where we were coming from and where we were going, he ordered the soldiers to let us pass, and they had to clear away the guns that had been positioned on the road that we had to pass through. The soldiers didn't like having to do that, but they obeyed and got rid of the guns and we were able to pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This Vukosavljevic, over the course of the next several days, did you have conversations with him regarding the situation in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. In the following days, I had an opportunity to meet with Captain Vukosavljevic on several occasions. One night we stayed the whole night in the dam. Nobody slept. We spent the entire night discussing the situation, the current situation, and the causes of the situation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he had been told about the situation in Visegrad prior to his arrival in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Vukosavljevic, at first, when we were captured, when he arrived to let us go, he was extremely angry and he did not like us. I spent this evening, this whole evening, with him. He asked me about the overall situation in the town. This was his major area of interest. I explained this to him. I explained the actual situation, because I realised that he obviously had a completely wrong picture of what had been going on in the town. And after that, he changed substantially. And, in fact, he did help us. He met some of our requests. So his relationship, his attitude towards us, changed 100 per cent after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What had he been told was happening in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, he told me first of all that he had been transferred urgently from Macedonia, where he had served as an officer of the JNA, to Serbia, and then immediately to Visegrad, with the order to take the dam and to secure it. He was also told that Muslims were committing horrible crimes there, slaughtering Serbs, roasting small children on spits, and so on and so forth. And this was the preconception that he had when he arrived there. After this talk with me, and I assume with some other people of Serbian ethnic background, he realised that this was not the actual real situation, that these were all things that had been invented by somebody. And then his attitude towards us changed. When I said "towards us," I mean the legal authorities and the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now move to day four. Were you called a second time to have a meeting with Yugoslav People's Army representatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: On the first day of our meeting with Ojdanic, nothing really was achieved, nothing special was achieved, because he wanted the representatives of both parties present there, both of the SDA and the SDS, the Democratic Action Party and the Serbian Democratic Party. Since members of the SDS were not present at the first meeting, he promised that he would make sure that SDS members were present on the next meeting the next day, together with the President, Brane Savovic. So what was agreed at the first meeting was that the second meeting would be held the next day. I arrived on time at that second meeting, but the other members had not yet arrived because there was quite a lot of shooting around the town and it was quite unsafe to travel. So the other members failed to arrive. I entered the room, the same room where the meeting was held the day before. I sat down at the table and waited for the other people to arrive. Officers, two or three officers of the JNA, were there. I said hello to them. I sat down and we did not talk at any length. And after a short while, another officer of the Yugoslav People's Army entered the room, carrying some military maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would there have been any way for these people to know who you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, if they had asked anyone who I was, somebody would have told them that. But I don't think that they knew. They did not ask me anything, so they did not know who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when this third officer walked into the room with the maps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The third officer brought the map, sat down at the table where I was sitting, right across me, it so happened, because there was an empty space there. He spread the map on the table, so the map was right in front of me. In the beginning, I just looked at this whole thing. I was not really interested in the proceedings. But then he explained to the other officers how far each of the units from Uzice got, how far they reached. And now this topic really got my -- got me interested. I was looking at what he was pointing at at the map and listening to what he was saying to the other officers. He explained to them, very briefly, showing them on the map the points where the units were, the points that the units had reached, saying, "This whole area is clean." "Another unit reached this such and such point. This is all clean." And so he went through the whole of the right bank of the river, indicating the points that the units had reached and saying, "This is all clean."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what is this a map of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: It was a military map. I know what a military map looks like, because I had the opportunity to hold it in my hands. There were blue and red arrows and signs. I am not really familiar with those signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it a map of Visegrad municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, indeed. It was a map of the Visegrad municipality. I knew every location. I knew all those places that the officer pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue. You were describing what the officer said about the right bank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. And at one point, he circled a location on the left bank of the river. He circled an area, saying, "This area we will clean tomorrow." I saw this, and I know -- I knew what the word "to clean" meant. And he indicated an area where about 4.000 Muslims lived. There were several groups of villages there, including the village where my father was born, and I knew that there were about 4.000 people there, and the word "to clean" was a term that was used in the sense of to clean it from -- of people, to remove all the people, to clean it in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You say that this place that was pointed to was a place that you were familiar with. Had you been to that place in the preceding days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any conflict going on in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No, no, there were no conflicts there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I was familiar with this location because my father was born there and my entire family, father, mother, brothers, sisters, their children, my wife, my children, were there. They were all there. And in the previous days, I had been going there, and I knew how many people there were. There were so many people there. It was crammed with people. If I may be allowed to give you an image, my father could not sleep. There was no room for him to sleep in his own house. They had to sleep elsewhere, in the car. So I knew just how many people there were, because I had been visiting this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Then I became paralysed, as we say in Bosnia. I was unable to move, because in a split second, I knew what the officer had pointed out. I knew what "to clean" meant, and I knew what would happen, what he was planning to do. And because so many people were there, including my entire family, I was paralysed for an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: And even after ten years, I don't feel comfortable describing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Colonel Ojdanic did arrive for the scheduled meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: When I insisted, in fact, I even cried. I was unable to say a word for an hour. My chin froze. I was unable to utter a single word. There were some foreign journalists there in the barracks. I spoke to them. Perhaps that had some impact on the development. But at any rate, they told me that the colonel would arrive for the negotiations, because before that, he had told us that he would not be arriving because there weren't enough people for him to actually conduct any negotiations. So the Colonel arrived, perhaps an hour later. In the meantime, the others came, the President of the Rudo municipality, Mr. Topalovic, and the SDA president for Rudo, Ramiz Abdem [phoen]. I was already there, and the colonel arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we get to that meeting, you described people being in the barracks and meeting some reporters. What barracks are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Uzamnica barracks, which is quite close to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe who you saw in the -- who were the people you were referring to when you saw there were people in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: These were the refugees from the town mostly and from the villages in the immediate vicinity of the barracks, but most of them were from the town, because they were afraid of the water coming. There was this hype that the water would be released, and they also knew that the army would be arriving. They took shelter in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: They were mostly Muslims. Perhaps 99.9 per cent of them were Muslims. I saw some that I recognised, but there were also some Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the reporter that you met, did you describe to this reporter what you had just seen earlier regarding the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. I, in fact, asked the reporters to stay there until the next day, explaining to them, saying to them that a genocide would take place in the vicinity of the town of Visegrad. He did not really trust me because he thought that I was one of the refugees there. When I explained to him that I was not a refugee, that I was there to take part in the negotiations with the colonel, that he was from the outside, and I also explained to him the functions that I held at the time, then they said, "All right, we'll stay there until the next day." I think that actually this was the crucial element that made the colonel arrive and take part in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd asked you to describe what happened during those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: You mean the reporters? We did not get into any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The negotiations with the colonel. Would you please describe the meeting with the colonel now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The colonel arrived. I already mentioned other people present. He is a pleasant person. He was in a good mood. He sat down at the table. He greeted us. And first he addressed me saying, "Do you have any particular problems?" referring to the situation that I had been in an hour ago and the fact that my family was there with all the other people in Brstanica. I said that I did not have any particular problems, that I had the same problems like everybody else. The president of the Rudo municipality was the first to speak at the meeting as the Democratic Action Party and the Serbian Democratic Party were able to reach an agreement and that there were no problems there and that the same type of agreement should be reached in Visegrad. I then spoke very briefly, insisting on the following point: that the JNA should protect this large group of people in Brstanica, that they should protect them so that they do not come to any harm. They were saying that there were no problems, there was nobody to protect them from, that they were sure that there would be no problems, but I knew that there could be a large-scale massacre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Up until this time, had the Yugoslav People's Army provided protection for any of the Muslim communities in the Visegrad municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: You mean in just the short term or in the period of, let's say, 20 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. I'm saying at the time that you're making this request. Was it because at present there was no protection for the Muslim settlements in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. This was the reason I sought the protection of the Yugoslav People's Army, because there was nobody else to provide such protection. They were the only ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did Colonel Ojdanic say when you made this request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Colonel Ojdanic first said -- because I asked for the protection of these people by the JNA, he said, "I don't know. I have my superiors too." Then after some further conversation, I asked him, "Does it mean that if we cannot have -- make sure that the SDS members are here at the negotiating table, does this mean that the Yugoslav People's Army will just sit back and watch the Muslim population being massacred?" And his response to this was, "All right. Tomorrow we will enter the town and we will protect this group of people," that I had mentioned, the people in Brstanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything else that occurred at that meeting of importance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, that was more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the meeting, I'd ask you to describe for the Chamber what happened regarding the protection that you had requested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: After the meeting, the colonel had to go urgently to Uzice. I went out and talked for a while with Captain Vukosavljevic. He was the commander of the dam. I told him what had happened, and he was already concerned about the developments. He was not present at the meeting, so I described very briefly what had happened, and I told him that the colonel promised that he would order the army to protect the population and to secure or, in other words, to take the town. So we said good-bye, and I went to this place where my parents lived, which is called Crnca. I spent the night there, and the next morning I phoned Captain Vukosavljevic at the dam, asking him what had happened with the promise that the colonel made last night about protecting the civilians, and he told me that there were some unforeseen problems and that the army was unable to do it that day, that they would do it the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you went to this village, did you see any signs that there was protection from the Yugoslav People's Army there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: On that day? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the day of the meeting when you went to this village, did you see any evidence that protection was being provided to these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No. No. Nobody from the Yugoslav People's Army was there. People were very scared. Their fate was uncertain, and they were really afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Vukosavljevic ever suggest to you that you contact Colonel Ojdanic again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: This happened on the day when the army was supposed to protect the civilians, according to his promise. Since the colonel notified us from Uzice that he would be unable to do this -- to do that on that day but the next day, I decided, although it was quite risky, to go there. I got into my car and rushed there. I met with Vukosavljevic and I asked him, "How come the army is not moving yet?" He said, "I don't know what's happening. Why don't you call Uzice? Call the colonel and insist that he fulfil his promise, the promise that he made the day before." And this is precisely what I did. He gave me the phone number. He also handed me the phone. So I called him. One of his officers answered the phone. I told him who I was, and I got the colonel on the line. I reminded him of the events, and I insisted for the army to go there on that day, that we were should not be waiting another day. And then he said, "Okay. Let Captain Vukosavljevic call me." And that's what I told him. He went to another office and called the colonel from there. I don't know what they were talking about. The conversation was not long. And he came back in a very good mood, and he told me, he said, "We got the approval from the colonel. We're going to move quickly. Let's get all those people from the villages and into the town." He put maybe 30 soldiers onto two trucks, and I got into his car with him. He drove a Lada Niva. So followed by two trucks, we went straight to Brstanica to let those people know that they should go to town and take shelter in the town as soon as possible, where they would be put under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. And that's what happened. We went there. The people had already got the news somehow - they knew that we would get there - and they gathered in the centre of the village of Brstanica in large numbers. Vukosavljevic insisted that this all be done very quickly, that columns be formed. There were some passenger vehicles. He wanted the old people to get into cars, and he wanted everybody to go to Visegrad immediately. That's what we ask. We organised everything as quickly as possible, formed the columns, and we headed towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is this on the date that the Uzice Corps actually enters the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe their arrival, where they came from, and the circumstances of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, the Uzice Corps came from the direction of Uzice, and that is on the right bank of the Drina from the direction of Serbia, the town of Uzice in Serbia; from several directions, actually. And they were fully equipped with the weapons that the JNA usually had. Apart from the standard so-called infantry weapons, there were tanks, guns, mortars, and so on. They had a full range of weaponry. The units were completely equipped, and they were coming in from different directions so that they covered the whole right bank of the River Drina, but they didn't enter the town straight away. They did this only one or two days later. So for one or two days, the town was completely empty. They entered town on the day that the people from Brstanica arrived; a little before them, perhaps an hour or two before. They took control of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did these people -- where were they made to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The problem was where to put up this large number of people, and Captain Vukosavljevic had no idea where to put them up. First of all, he thought we'd put them up in the hotel. The hotel's name was the Hotel Visegrad. But when he saw there were many more people than he had assumed, he said, "Let's go to the football stadium." And that's what happened. He took the column off to the football stadium. I stayed behind because, before we came into the town, you could hear shooting. The shooting was fairly intense along the road which we were to take. So the captain then said to me - and there were two other men with me who were sitting in his car, in the Niva car - "You stay here, I'll go on ahead to see what's happening, what all the shooting is about." And he went off in the direction the shooting was coming from, and we stayed on further down alone. In the meantime, the people had already arrived, went into the town and went off towards the stadium, so that I arrived at the stadium when all the people were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were assembled in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At the stadium, there were about four thousand, perhaps four and a half thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did somebody from the Yugoslav People's Army address these 4.000 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The people were addressed by -- he introduced himself as the commander of the locality, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic. He used a loudspeaker, a megaphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that the first time you had seen Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I saw him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to his speech, did you go and try to speak with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Vukosavljevic, who went with us - in fact, introduced me to Jovanovic - he said, "This man's name is such and such. This is his post." And then the other one said, "I'm Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic, the commander of the locality." But he was a little arrogant. He didn't take me seriously, and he said, "You move away and let me hear from two or three of the citizens from amongst the people. Go and call two or three of the people." And that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you present during his address to the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. I was a little further off, 10 to 15 metres away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as best as you can remember, would you please relate to the Court what it was he said to these 4.000 Muslims assembled in the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I remember what he said. He said the following. Actually, he started off by introducing himself. He said who he was. He said he was the commander of the place and that they were to listen carefully to what he was going to say. And what he said was the following: He said that in a village -- that if a single shot was fired in any of the villages, he would raze the house to the ground, and if a soldier were wounded or shot in any of the villages, he would raze the whole village to the ground. He also said that he had the units of the White Eagles under his command, the Beli Orlovi. Otherwise those were the units that were most feared by the Muslims. They were terribly afraid of them. And that if anybody had any weapons, that they should turn them in; if they had not got these weapons with them, they could bring them in tomorrow; and that they were free to leave, go back to their houses. But he also said where they were allowed to go and where not. So he enumerated all the places where they could go and those that they could not go to, and he said that where -- the areas his units covered, "You can go there," whereas he didn't offer any guarantees for any of the other places, if people went to any of the other places. So that was more or less the gist of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Because it's so important, I would ask you, to the best that you're able, tell us exactly what he said regarding the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, he just addressed one or two sentences. He said that the units of the White Eagles were under his command, or "are under my command." That's what he said. "And so take care of what you do."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what places specifically did he say Muslims were permitted to go and what places were they not permitted to go, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I remember that too, because I knew all these localities. They were -- I was well-acquainted with them. On the right bank of the river, he said that we were permitted to go up to the village of Musici but not further on, including the village of Musici. So that village was sort of -- it was better not to go to the village of Musici, but up to that village, downstream from the town. And on the left bank, he enumerated all the villages in order, Sumchaila [phoen], Jelasci, Hamzici, Brstanica, and said that we were permitted to go there, the people were allowed to go back to those villages. So what happened was that the people from the right bank, from the places that the colonel did not enumerate, went to the left bank, returned to the left bank, stayed with relatives or friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And these locations on the right bank, were some of these the same locations that you had heard referred to as having been cleaned the day before in Uzamnica Barracks -- or, I'm sorry, in the meeting the day before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was precisely those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the people were not permitted to return there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the 4.000 people in the stadium were searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: When the colonel finished speaking, he explained that the people had to pass by in columns, and the soldiers did -- made three or four checkpoints, set up three or four checkpoints. The people would pass by them. They would ask if anybody had any weapons it turn in, and once the people had passed the checkpoint, they were free to go to the localities that the colonel had said were safe. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was every person in the stadium searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At the beginning, they were diligent in their searches. But as there were so many people who were hurrying, it was just a routine sort of quick search, not in any great detail as had been the case at first. For example, they didn't search me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a gun with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At that time, I really did have a pistol on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you do --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: It was a Zastava pistol, 762 calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you do with that pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, as the town was full of soldiers, it was like when you come out of the cinema, when the audience leaves a cinema. I was frightened of what I would do if somebody found the pistol on me. I found Captain Vukosavljevic and I handed him the pistol, telling him to keep it for me because if I was searched and found with a pistol on me, it would mean my head. He took the pistol and a few days later sent me a certificate. He issued a certificate saying I had handed him the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just for the record, what was the ethnic background of Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: He was of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you do after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: After the meeting, the colonel spoke to me briefly and told me to report to him at the hotel. And that's what I did. I went to the Visegrad Hotel which was in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which colonel was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic. Actually he was Lieutenant-Colonel, I'm sorry. Not Colonel; Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately what time was this when you went to the Visegrad Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Not long after the speech delivered by commander Jovanovic. I stayed on for a few moments to see if my family was there and then went off to the hotel. When I got to the hotel, I was told to wait by an officer who met me there. He said that the commander would not be receiving me straight away, that I had to wait a while. And while I was waiting by the reception desk, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic turned up along with Branimir Savovic, who was wearing a military camouflage uniform. As they went in to where I was supposed to go to see the commander, I was told shortly that the commander would be unable to receive me on that day and that I was to return the next day. So I left the hotel and went to the place where my family was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please remind us who Mr. Savovic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Branimir Savovic was in fact the President of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, for the Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I left Visegrad on the 16th of May at 12.00 noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please describe for the Court the circumstances under which you left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: As the army had taken control of the town, and they were to leave Visegrad on the 20th of May, I think, it was not very safe towards the end of the time for their departure. It was unsafe. And I felt that it was not safe for me or my family to stay, and we decided to leave town. But that was no easy thing to do, because at all the exits there were checkpoints and people were not allowed to leave. What I did was to ask the Vice-President of the Serbian Democratic Party, one of the vice-presidents, his name was Stanko Pecikoza, who was an influential man both in the party and in town generally, to take me and my family out of town, towards Uzice. That was the only exit road open, taking you out of town. He explained to us in great detail when we -- where we should gather, when the departure would be scheduled, and he took us through the checkpoints. There were two checkpoints, one in Dobrun and the other in Dabric on the road to Uzice. Then he issued instructions as to what we were to do once we crossed into Serbia, how we were to proceed. And we carried on towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this man who helped sneak you out of Visegrad, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: He was a Serb, an influential Serb in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know where he is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he died. He is dead. He was a good man. And as far as I know, he was liquidated by the members of the SDS a little after the time he took me and my family out of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you began your testimony by saying that the parties were formed in Visegrad. And you mentioned, if I understood you correctly, that the two strongest parties were the Party of Democratic Action and the SDS party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us which of these two parties was formed first, established first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't say for sure. I don't have that information. But both parties were set up in a short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You're not sure that -- whether the SDS was formed before the SDS [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there any other national party, ethnic party, in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, if you can call them nationalist parties, there were other parties where the members were predominantly one ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we say, for example, that in the SDA party, of which you were a member, there were Serbs too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Or that there were Muslims in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No. There weren't any Muslims in the SDS either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These, then, were nationalist parties, were they not? Ethnically based; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, if you say so, then all right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, that would emanate from your answer. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, just one moment. When both of you are speaking the same language, you present terrible problems for the interpreters. Please pause after the answer before you start your question. And, sir, would you please pause before you start your answer after the end of the question? Otherwise, the interpreters lose you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the town of Visegrad itself, in view of the ethnic composition of the population, could you tell me whether it is true that in posts of leadership, in executive power, the courts and legislation, you had representatives of both the two major ethnic groups; that is to say, the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After the multi-party elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. I asked before, before the multi-party elections, up until the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: My answer is yes. Before as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us that the multi-party elections, as far as Visegrad is concerned, ended -- resulted in a majority for the Democratic Action Party, with 27 seats compared to 13 seats from the SDS. Did this correspond to the national structure of the population and the ratio between the Muslims and Serbs in town? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Roughly it did. The ratio was roughly the same, like the national composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After the establishment of local power and authority, after the elections that you mentioned, were there any changes in the leadership structure and leadership posts in the Visegrad area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. Changes did take place in the municipal organs of authority. In the other structures there were no changes. For example, in the companies, the directors or managers weren't replaced. If you were a manager before the elections, you went on being the manager after the elections. All that changed was the structure I mentioned in the municipality, the executive council, board of the municipality, and the secretariats, the organs of power and authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, the organs of power and authority. Was it under the competence of these authorities to replace managers of companies, according to the laws that were in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I can't be a hundred per cent certain, but I think that the authorities could have replaced them had they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the president of the municipality could replace a manager of a company in Visegrad; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No, he couldn't do that directly. He couldn't issue a direct order to have these people replaced, but the Assembly did have authority over the nomination and appointment of certain directors or managers of companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you mean the directors of the communal enterprises, the utilities, or the other socially-owned companies as they were called at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, to quote an example, they could exert changes on the utilities companies and the companies close to the state structures, attached to the state structure, but they could also replace other managers as well. I know, for example, because I was one of the managers. I was a manager myself, a director. I know that they talked to my colleagues, and people were fairly afraid as to whether the new authorities would replace the directors or not. I remember that. We were -- all had this qualm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. You were the director of one particular company. I won't mention which one, but it wasn't an utilities company. It was a socially-owned company. And you were not appointed by either the municipal assembly, nor could it relieve you of your duties nor appoint you to another post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether after the establishment of these new authorities after the first multi-party elections, at any post of leadership in the courts such as the president of the court, the president of the municipality or executive board, were they Serbs or were all these posts held by Muslims, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, this corresponded roughly -- that is to say, I know when negotiations took place with respect to the nomination and appointment of people to fill these responsible posts. I know that a basic criterion for this was the number of votes gained at the elections, and that's how those structures were established, the new authorities after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question was a concrete one. The president of the municipality was a Muslim, was he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The president of the executive board likewise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you who everybody was. Yes, the president was a Muslim. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This was a prominent leadership post after the president of the municipality. What about the president of the court in Visegrad after the elections? Who was he? Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think he was, yes. That is to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, these are facts that we can ascertain. But you said that this corresponded to the structure. How did this correspond if all the leadership posts were held by Muslims? How then do you believe that the Serbs had a share in the posts of leadership, according to the election results?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. The president of the municipality, as the highest authority, came from the ranks of the SDA party. The vice-president was from the ranks of the SDS party, and her name was Jelisavka. I can't remember the lady's surname, but she used to be a teacher at the primary school I attended. Now, the president of the executive board was an SDA member, and the vice-president was from the SDA, and he was Slobodan Klipe. So this is how the parity ratio worked, power distribution. For example, the president of one of the municipal bodies, I think the registry office, land registry office, was a Serb also. His name was Sinisa Ceho, I think. And that's why I say more or less why this parity was reflected on the posts of leadership. The election results were reflected on the composition of the leadership posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the only Serb whom you considered to have been in a prime post was the president of the land registry office. Is that true? If so, let me tell you that that post did not exist. Perhaps he was head of the land registry office so that that was the only post that a Serb held, just that post with the land registry office, whereas in all the other posts Serbs were either assistants or deputies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, yes. I have remembered what I have just told you. That's what I recall. But I continue to claim and I know that it was agreed upon that the SDA party and the Serbian Democratic Party -- and as I say, I attended some of those meetings when they were deciding on the distribution of power and authority on the basis of the electoral results. That's how it worked. That's how the system functioned. An agreement did exist. It was signed and everybody was happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you consider that the SDS was happy, was pleased, satisfied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, they accepted the agreement that was reached. The agreement was accepted by both parties and signed, and they put forward these people. For example, for the vice-president of the municipality and the vice-president of the executive board and so on and so forth, they nominated people from amongst their ranks, and that is why I say that I consider that they accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Up until this authority was established, did the statute of your municipality envisage a two-thirds majority deciding upon all major issues according to the statute?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I can't be quite sure of that. I can't say with any certainty, but yes, certainly some questions must have been decided, and to be decided by a two-third majority vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, it's 1.00, lunch. But when we resume, do you think we might advance to the relevant period, which was in 1992? What is the relevance of all this? Was it to provide some sort of motive for the Serbs to throw out the Muslims? What is its relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I don't mean to justify anyone or anything, any act. But I considered, and I am drawing to a close. I'm reaching the end. I just have a few more questions on that area and then we'll go back to April 1992 and continue from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It better be relevant, though, Mr. Domazet. We are not going to run into a political argument about what was fair and what was not fair back in 1990. That has nothing to do with this case. So if you can say you will have two questions, we'll allow you two questions, but we want to get on with what is relevant, which, as you agree, is April 1992. We will resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just before we do break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Over the weekend a situation arose regarding two witnesses, and I will be seeking some protective measures for those two witnesses. One of them is scheduled to testify tomorrow. I wonder if the Court would entertain an oral application followed by papers or grant me time to try to put together the affidavit and the motion this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is no need to put it in writing, Mr. Groome, but we do want some reason why this is being done late, and in particular, if you want something more than facial pixilation and pseudonym, you will have to justify it with something fairly substantial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's nothing more than that, Your Honour, and there is an explanation why it is late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, on my desk when I got back was a motion seeking leave to call an additional expert witness. May I suggest that this appalling American habit of putting everything in writing, which has been imposed upon this Tribunal, is not one that we need follow in every case? What I suggest you do is you speak to Mr. Domazet about it, give him a copy of the report. If he's got some problems with it, then we'll hear it when we are about to finish at 4.00 one afternoon or something like that. But we do not need this sort of motion in writing. I don't know why we were ever inflicted with it, but I rather suspect that Judge McDonald had something to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. You proceed, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to conclude, and as I have already said, I have perhaps two more questions relating to the period. First question: Are you aware of the fact that the Assembly that you spoke about changed its statute and repelled the provision about the two-thirds majority required for certain decisions, that this was done precisely by the Muslim majority in the Assembly, that this decision was -- that this provision was changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. I don't think that this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another thing: Are you aware of the fact that the Serb deputies left the Assembly and no longer took part in its work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, this might have happened sporadically when they were unhappy with certain items or provisions. Some deputies may have left the Assembly, but then they would come again and take part in the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, we obviously are not talking about the same thing. But I don't want to dwell upon it any longer. I would now like to go to the period spring 1992, that you spoke about at length and in some detail today. One of the questions put to you referred to the Territorial Defence and the fact that weapons were seized -- weapons were seized from the Territorial Defence. Was the Territorial Defence in Visegrad composed only of -- both of Serbs and of Muslims or just some of those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was composed both of Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that if the weapons were seized from the Territorial Defence in Visegrad, that all the members of the Territorial Defence no longer had access to weapons, regardless of their ethnicity, Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke about the fact that Serbs were able to obtain weapons in some way. Do you have any specific knowledge as to who obtained the weapons and in which way, based on your direct knowledge or direct observation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I personally did not see weapons being distributed to Serbs, if that's what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you -- do you know that the Muslims did the same thing; in other words, that they also obtained weapons in this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At that time, some Muslims did obtain weapons by actually buying those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, was the chief of the MUP or the police, was it Seval Murtic, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anyone - I mean specifically the JNA that you referred to when you spoke about the Territorial Defence - did anyone interfere with the weapons held by the police? Did they disarm the police or ask them to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I cannot state this with any certainty, but I don't think so. I think that the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned that you have personal knowledge that Serbs were called up for military exercises because you had the opportunity to see this in your company. Can you tell us who sent those call-up papers and who is in charge of sending such call-up papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I do not know who sent those papers. I just heard from what people who actually went to those exercises told me. They gave me this as an excuse as to why they have to be absent from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it your knowledge or do you remember that it was the military department that was in charge of sending such papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember who was, at the time, the chief or the head of the military department in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: At the time when the call-up papers were sent out, I do not remember who was the head of the office, of the department, but I do know it was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you sure? Do you know the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No, I do not know his name, but I am absolutely certain that he was a Serb, because no Muslims worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us stay with the military department. Are you aware of the fact that Muslims seized some weapons belonging to the military department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about an incident in the quarry around about the 4th of April. Could you please tell us more about it? You said that some people were shot at. Do you know who opened fire and for what reason, and what was the conclusion of this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I could only make an assumption as to who opened fire. I knew the people who were shot at very well. And immediately after the event, they told me about it, and the outcome of the shooting was that everybody left their posts there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Those who worked there. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Today you spoke about the events a day or two after that when mortar fire was opened on Visegrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also talked about the fact that the Muslim areas and the town centre were targeted. Can you please tell me which areas in Visegrad were purely Muslim? Were there any such areas, in fact, at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: There were quite a few areas which were purely Muslim. There can be no doubt about that. In addition to the town centre, Nezuci was one the first villages to be targeted. It is a village quite close to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I know, the dam is quite far away from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you claim that mortar fire was opened both on the town centre and areas around the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I was present in the town centre when the shells fell. As for this other thing, I want to say that this was not close to the dam. The village of Nezuci was targeted. In addition to the villagers, there were quite a few refugees there, and I was personally visited by a man who asked me for some gasoline to transport his wife to the hospital because she was wounded in the mortar attack. This woman was 11 months' pregnant [sic] at the time. There was another person, a Muslim priest, who was also wounded, and he was also taken to Gorazde, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talk about the persons who were wounded, do you know whether anyone was killed in any of these attacks in Visegrad and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: There were some people who died; specifically this woman that I mentioned. She did not survive. I know that quite a few people were wounded. I'm not sure about the persons who were killed, as to their number, but some people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In Visegrad itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: In Visegrad, yes, but to a lesser extent. I am now talking about this village of Nezuci, which is close to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about the negotiations with the representatives of the SDS which were mediated by the JNA, you said that the meeting took place somewhere in Kosovo Polje. Why was the meeting not held in Visegrad, or in other words, where were those SDS representatives at the time when you organised this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: The meeting that you're referring to was held at Kosovo Polje. It was not organised with the mediation of the army. I spoke directly with Branimir Savovic, who was the SDS president. He was in Visegradska Banja, on the phone, and we agreed to have a meeting at Kosovo Polje because it was roughly halfway between Visegradska Banja and the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that at that time, Brane Savovic and the SDS members were in Visegradska Banja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: As far as I know -- maybe I could give you a wider answer. I knew the phone numbers in Visegradska Banja very well, and Savovic answered the phone that -- the phone number that I dialed, but I think that at that time I think that he was actually in a village further up from Visegradska Banja. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know why Savovic and the others were not in Visegrad but in Visegradska Banja or in the villages nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I think that they went, left the town of their own volition and went elsewhere because they wanted to occupy the town from the positions around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you think that they left the city, the town, in order to be able to go back and occupy it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs in the town at the time, or did a certain number or perhaps the majority or even all of them, did they leave the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Most of them left the town, and some remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is the period before the incident involving the releasing of the water from the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. But we met at Kosovo Polje one day after the water was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just -- I just want to -- we are talking about the Serbs leaving the town. When did they leave the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the witness is behaving very well. He's pausing. You're not. Just give it a break. You've got your earphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You can probably hear it. It's a good test, if I may say so, if you see that the typing is finished, you know then that the interpretation is finished. But please do pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can I then take it to mean the following: When the threat was made that the water would be released, that mostly Muslims remained in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, mostly, but there was a substantial number of Serbs left too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talked about the Uzamnica Barracks and the fact that many people had taken refuge there and that perhaps 99 per cent of these people were Muslims, were these the same people that remained in Visegrad and who left Visegrad, who fled Visegrad, because of the danger that the water might be released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As regards the releasing of the water, you told us today that this had been done by a man by the name of Murat Sabanovic, and you said that he had got there on his own initiative, but you left it at that. Could you please clarify it, what did you mean when you said that, if you still maintain that he went to the hydroelectric power plant on his own initiative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. I did use this term advisedly, "on his own initiative." He took with him a group of his friends, neighbours, perhaps some of his relatives. They organised themselves in their village, since the situation was such that they felt this overall insecurity, and the people in the villages just organised themselves in order to protect themselves and their families, their villages. And he went with a group of his relatives, neighbours and so on, to the dam, and this is what I meant when I said that he did it on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So he went to the dam with a group of his relatives and neighbours. Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as you know, do you know if there was anyone on the dam to defend the dam? Do you think -- do you know whether the dam was defended by anyone with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: No. There was nobody to offer any resistance. The dam was not guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as you remember, how long did it last? How long did Murat Sabanovic and his friends and relatives hold the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, not to be too precise, I think about four days, four or five days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During that time, did the police in Visegrad take any measures to resolve this problem in any way, to arrest Murat Sabanovic and the rest of the people who had taken the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, because these events were happening very fast. A lot of things happened every day. I don't know whether they did anything, but I do know that there was no danger, that he and his group were no danger to the personnel at the dam or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? How do you know that he posed no danger to the personnel at the dam, if we know that he was armed and that they held -- that they were armed and that they held the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I do not have any specific proof. But on the basis of the actual situation, he did not make any threats to anyone, any of the employees on the dam, and since the people who worked -- also, the people who worked on the dam said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is what you heard from the people who worked on the dam, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yet if the fact that he held the dam with the weapons, if this was not a great risk, do you also maintain that the threat of releasing the water was no -- that it was not a great threat, neither for Visegrad nor for other places down river from Visegrad on the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I do not make any such claims because I'm not an expert. But as far as I know, since I am of the same profession, I was able to conclude that no major damage could have been caused, particularly in light of the fact that the next dam further down river was empty and that it was possible for this dam to hold the water from the previous dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know -- are you not familiar with the fact that this river, that this lake, was emptied at the time precisely because there was a danger that Murat Sabanovic might release the water from the previous dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was the reason why this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more about the incident when 12 uniformed police officers of Serb ethnic background were arrested? You said that perhaps half of them were in the police. You said up until ten days before the event. Am I correct in my memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Something like that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please explain what happened in the ten-day period before this event? Did they cease being members of the police or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was perhaps 10 or 15 days before. I cannot be much more specific. The SDS asked for the police force to be split up. I attended some of the meetings where they demanded that the police be split up into the Serbian force and the Muslim force. And since they had a lot of influence over the Serbs, ethnic Serbs, some ten days before the shooting they directly were in charge of most of the Serb police officers, which means that most of them were already under the command of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If possible, could you explain this to us in a little more detail? How was it possible for one portion of the police force to be separate in one and the same town and have a separate command structure, if I understood you correctly? Could you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: In concrete terms, the demands that were made was that there be two police forces with two headquarters and for this newly established police force that they wanted to establish - that is, they envisaged - they had set aside a building next to the new bridge, on the right bank, about a kilometre away from the centre of town. That building that was to become the headquarters belonged to a company which was in charge of roads. It was the road administration company. And I know that they wanted this to become their police station. And that's why I said a moment ago what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But this did not actually come about; is that right? It didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: There was no political agreement for this to be implemented nor was there agreement from the competent authorities. I think that the main police administration was in Sarajevo, and they did not give the go-ahead for that. No such agreement was reached. But nevertheless, they did so on their own initiative. But they didn't have their command headquarters in that particular building, the one they had asked for during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, if I understood you correctly, among the group of people arrested, a certain number, almost half of them, were active-duty policemen, is that right, or Serbs? They were Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were they arrested because they were with another group of Serbs or were no longer policemen, or was there another reason, if you happen to know what the reason was, because you did speak about the reasons earlier on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: As far as I know, they no longer went to work regularly. They no longer went to the police station regularly to take up their duties there. And as they were in the company of people who were armed and wore uniforms but did not belong to any regular organisation, I think that that was the reason they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When they were arrested, I assume that they were taken to the police station. Were they all detained - that is to say, the policemen and the rest who were not policemen - and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, they were all detained. I know that for sure. And then after five or six days -- five, six, or seven days later - I'm not quite sure of the time - they were handed over to the Yugoslav People's Army at the dam; that is to say, they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Six to seven days after they were arrested; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did they spend all that time at the police station or at the dam or both at the police station and on the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't as well acquainted with those affairs. I know that they were at the police station. But as that area was shelled, then people didn't stay there for any length of time or move around, and I think that that was the reason they were transferred to the left bank as prisoners, to accompany their company building, and then sent from there to the dam. That's what I seem to recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But the police force didn't change its headquarters from the locality that you said was in danger of being shelled. The police force stayed on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: Yes. I think the police force stayed on there, that locality, at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The group on the dam was released, and it spent the last days on the dam. But the dam was held by Murat Sabanovic. Now, how can you explain the fact that they came under his command and control, that is to say that they become his prisoners if they were arrested by the regular police force? How did they come to be under his control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I didn't say that during those last days; that is to say, during the last two days, I communicated with those people, and I know about that. On the last day or perhaps the last two days, they were put up at the Granit construction company, and nearby there was a restaurant, and that's where they were. I know that full well because I was there. And one of the prisoners from that place talked on the telephone with Branimir Savovic. I know that for sure. As for the rest, I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, you were conducting negotiations and you were probably well acquainted with the overall situation, were you not? Now, I asked you how it could have come about that on the last few days or the very last day they came to be in the hands of ^ Murat Sabanovic and his group, the group that held the dam. How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I don't know that they were ever in his hands, as you have just said. What I know is what I have told you. I know that when people left the town, when the water was released and when the army was coming in, they were taken in a vehicle in the direction of Gorazde, towards Gorazde, because that's where the population withdrew to. Everybody went up there, to Gorazde. They were withdrawing towards Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you give the Prosecution a tape on which, among others, you had conversations taped of these people, these people who were arrested or detained, a tape where they spoke about-- speak about those days and the conditions prevailing, the conditions under which they were taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG22
utterances.text: I remember handing over a videotape to the investigator. Is that the term, the right term? I don't know. But I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, let's get this very clear. The investigators are not part of -- they're not part of the Tribunal as such. They're not our investigators. They are the Prosecution's investigators. Now, if you want to get this tape from the Prosecution, you only have to ask for it, I would have thought. I don't know why we're spending so much time with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
